name: Plague of Mursili
what: An epidemic brought home by Egyptian prisoners of war that raged in the Hittite kingdom for some twenty years.
why: King Mursili II's prayers blaming it on his father's broken oath are among the oldest written reactions to an epidemic.

sources.cite: Bryce, T. (2005). The Kingdom of the Hittites. Oxford University Press (Plague Prayers of Mursili II).

name: Plague of Athens
what: An unidentified epidemic that killed perhaps a quarter of Athens while it sat behind its Long Walls during the Peloponnesian War.
why: It killed Pericles, and Thucydides, who caught it and lived, described how fear dissolved law and religion in the city.

sources.cite: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 2.47-54.

name: Antonine Plague
what: Probably smallpox, carried home by legions returning from Mesopotamia; it struck the empire at its height.
why: The first pandemic in recorded history; Harper reads it as the moment the Roman climate optimum and good luck ran out.

sources.cite: Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton University Press.

name: Plague of Cyprian
what: A pandemic, possibly a viral haemorrhagic fever, named for the bishop of Carthage who described it.
why: It hit during the Crisis of the Third Century, and Christian care for the sick may have helped the church grow.

sources.cite: Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton University Press.

name: Plague of Justinian
what: The first known pandemic of Yersinia pestis, reaching Constantinople in 542 and returning in waves until about 750.
why: Historians disagree sharply on its toll: Harper sees an empire-breaking catastrophe, Mordechai et al. see far smaller effects.

sources.cite: Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton University Press.
Mordechai, L. et al. (2019). The Justinianic Plague: An inconsequential pandemic? PNAS 116(51).

name: Black Death
what: Plague spread from the steppe to the Crimea, then by ship and caravan across the Mediterranean, the Near East and Europe.
why: It killed something like 30 to 60 percent of Europe and raised wages for the survivors, reshaping labour, faith and power.

sources.cite: Benedictow, O. J. (2004). The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History. Boydell Press.
Spyrou, M. A. et al. (2022). The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia. Nature 606, 718-724.
Dols, M. W. (1977). The Black Death in the Middle East. Princeton University Press.

name: English sweating sickness
what: A fast-killing fever of unknown cause that struck England in five waves and then vanished.
why: It could kill within hours and mostly hit the well-off, then disappeared so completely that its cause is still a mystery.

sources.cite: Dyer, A. (1978). The influence of bubonic plague in England 1500-1667; Wylie, J. and Collier, L. (1981). The English sweating sickness (Sudor Anglicus): a reappraisal. Journal of the History of Medicine 36(4).

name: Smallpox in the Aztec Empire
what: Smallpox reached Tenochtitlan in 1520 with Narvaez's expedition and killed the emperor Cuitlahuac among many others.
why: Without immunity, the epidemic did more than Spanish steel to decide the fall of Tenochtitlan.

sources.cite: Crosby, A. W. (1972). The Columbian Exchange. Greenwood.

name: Cocoliztli epidemic
what: A haemorrhagic fever that killed perhaps 80 percent of the native population of central Mexico.
why: Acuna-Soto links its timing to a megadrought in the tree-ring record, an early disease-climate link.

sources.cite: Acuna-Soto, R. et al. (2002). Megadrought and megadeath in 16th century Mexico. Emerging Infectious Diseases 8(4).

name: Great Plague of London
what: The last major outbreak of plague in England, recorded week by week in the Bills of Mortality.
why: Pepys watched it from the city, and Newton went home to Woolsthorpe to wait it out.

sources.cite: Porter, S. (2009). The Great Plague. Amberley; Bills of Mortality, City of London.

name: Great Plague of Marseille
what: Plague arrived on the trading ship Grand-Saint-Antoine from the Levant and killed about half of Marseille.
why: Merchants pushed to unload the cargo for a fair, and the quarantine wall built afterwards became a model for later plague control.

sources.cite: Biraben, J.-N. (1975). Les hommes et la peste en France et dans les pays europeens et mediterraneens. Mouton.

name: Yellow fever in Saint-Domingue
what: Yellow fever destroyed most of the army Napoleon sent to retake Saint-Domingue.
why: McNeill argues mosquitoes helped make Haiti independent and pushed Napoleon to sell Louisiana.

sources.cite: McNeill, J. R. (2010). Mosquito Empires: Ecology and War in the Greater Caribbean, 1620-1914. Cambridge University Press.

name: First cholera pandemic
what: Cholera spread out of the Ganges delta along British military and trade routes to Southeast Asia, the Gulf and Russia.
why: The first of seven cholera pandemics, and the start of modern public health through sewers and clean water.

sources.cite: Pollitzer, R. (1959). Cholera. World Health Organization Monograph 43.

name: Third plague pandemic
what: Plague moved from Yunnan to Hong Kong in 1894, then by steamship to every inhabited continent.
why: Yersin identified the plague bacillus in Hong Kong in 1894, and India suffered most of the deaths.

sources.cite: WHO, Plague fact sheet; Echenberg, M. (2007). Plague Ports. NYU Press.

name: 1889-1890 pandemic
what: A respiratory pandemic first reported in St Petersburg that circled the world in about four months on railways and steamships.
why: The first pandemic to spread at the speed of modern transport; its cause, influenza or a coronavirus, is still debated.

sources.cite: Valleron, A.-J. et al. (2010). Transmissibility and geographic spread of the 1889 influenza pandemic. PNAS 107(19).

name: 1918 influenza pandemic
what: An H1N1 influenza that spread with troops at the end of the First World War, unusually deadly to young adults.
why: Where it started is disputed; Kansas, the British camp at Etaples and northern China all have advocates.

sources.cite: Spreeuwenberg, P. et al. (2018). Reassessing the global mortality burden of the 1918 influenza pandemic. American Journal of Epidemiology 187(12).
Johnson, N. and Mueller, J. (2002). Updating the accounts: global mortality of the 1918-1920 Spanish influenza pandemic. Bulletin of the History of Medicine 76(1).

name: HIV/AIDS pandemic
what: HIV-1 group M spread from Kinshasa in the 1920s along railways and river routes, then worldwide from the 1970s.
why: Recognised only in 1981, decades after it began spreading; about 42 million people have died of it.

sources.cite: Faria, N. R. et al. (2014). The early spread and epidemic ignition of HIV-1 in human populations. Science 346(6205).
UNAIDS Global AIDS Update (2024).

name: COVID-19 pandemic
what: A coronavirus first identified in Wuhan that spread worldwide within three months.
why: About 7 million deaths were reported to WHO; excess-death estimates run three to four times higher.

sources.cite: WHO COVID-19 dashboard, deaths reported to WHO.
The Economist excess-deaths model (2023).

name: Great Famine
what: Years of cold and endless rain ruined harvests across northern Europe, followed by cattle plague.
why: It ended the medieval population boom and left a generation weakened thirty years before the Black Death.

sources.cite: Jordan, W. C. (1996). The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century. Princeton University Press.

name: Russian famine of 1601-1603
what: Frosts in summer 1601 destroyed three harvests running and killed perhaps a third of Muscovy.
why: It opened the Time of Troubles, Russia's near-collapse before the Romanovs.

sources.cite: Verosub, K. L. and Lippman, J. (2008). Global impacts of the 1600 eruption of Peru's Huaynaputina volcano. Eos 89(15).
Dunning, C. S. L. (2001). Russia's First Civil War: The Time of Troubles and the Founding of the Romanov Dynasty. Penn State Press.

name: Great Finnish famine
what: Cold during the late Maunder Minimum ruined harvests in Finland and Estonia.
why: Roughly a quarter to a third of Finland died, proportionally one of the worst famines in European history.

sources.cite: Jutikkala, E. (1955). The great Finnish famine in 1696-97. Scandinavian Economic History Review 3(1).

name: Irish famine of 1740-1741
what: The Great Frost of 1739-40 froze rivers and killed the potato crop in the ground.
why: Proportionally as deadly as the better-known famine a century later, and nearly forgotten.

sources.cite: Dickson, D. (1997). Arctic Ireland: The Extraordinary Story of the Great Frost and Forgotten Famine of 1740-41. White Row.

name: Bengal famine of 1770
what: Drought and East India Company revenue collection combined to starve Bengal, recently taken over by the Company.
why: Estimates run from about one to ten million deaths, and the scandal helped bring the Company under Parliament.

sources.cite: Sen, A. (1981). Poverty and Famines. Oxford University Press.
O Grada, C. (2009). Famine: A Short History. Princeton University Press.

name: Tenmei famine
what: Cold summers and the Asama eruption ruined rice harvests across northern Japan.
why: Rice riots followed in Edo and Osaka, and the shogunate answered with the Kansei reforms.

sources.cite: Kikuchi, I. (1997). Kinsei no kikin (Famines of early modern Japan); Jansen, M. (2000). The Making of Modern Japan. Harvard.

name: Chalisa famine
what: A failed monsoon devastated north India in the same years the Laki eruption chilled the northern hemisphere.
why: Grove ties it to a run of strong El Nino years at the end of the 18th century.

sources.cite: Grove, R. H. (2007). The Great El Nino of 1789-93 and its global consequences. Medieval History Journal 10(1-2).

name: Mist Hardships
what: Fluorine from the Laki eruption poisoned Iceland's grass, killing most of its livestock.
why: About a fifth of Iceland's people died; Denmark briefly considered evacuating the island.

sources.cite: Thordarson, T. and Self, S. (2003). Atmospheric and environmental effects of the 1783-1784 Laki eruption. Journal of Geophysical Research 108(D1).

name: Year Without a Summer
what: After the Tambora eruption, snow fell in June in New England and harvests failed across Europe and China.
why: Bread riots and emigration followed, and a wet summer by Lake Geneva produced Frankenstein.

sources.cite: Oppenheimer, C. (2003). Climatic, environmental and human consequences of the largest known historic eruption: Tambora volcano (Indonesia) 1815. Progress in Physical Geography 27(2).
Wood, G. D. (2014). Tambora: The Eruption That Changed the World. Princeton University Press.

name: Great Irish Famine
what: Potato blight destroyed the staple crop while food was still exported from Ireland.
why: A million died and another million emigrated; Ireland's population has still not recovered to its 1841 level.

sources.cite: O Grada, C. (2009). Famine: A Short History. Princeton University Press.

name: Great Famine of 1876-1878
what: Monsoon failure across south and west India while grain was exported and relief kept minimal.
why: Davis pairs it with the North China famine of the same El Nino years as a lesson in how policy turns drought into famine.

sources.cite: Davis, M. (2001). Late Victorian Holocausts: El Nino Famines and the Making of the Third World. Verso.

name: Northern Chinese Famine of 1876-1879
what: Drought across Shanxi, Henan and neighbouring provinces in the same El Nino years that struck India.
why: One of the deadliest famines in history, in a Qing state already weakened by the Taiping war.

sources.cite: Davis, M. (2001). Late Victorian Holocausts: El Nino Famines and the Making of the Third World. Verso.

name: Soviet famine of 1930-1933 (Holodomor)
what: Forced collectivisation and grain requisitions starved Ukraine, Kazakhstan and the Volga.
why: A famine made by policy; in Ukraine it is remembered as the Holodomor.

sources.cite: Applebaum, A. (2017). Red Famine: Stalin's War on Ukraine. Doubleday.

name: Bengal famine of 1943
what: Wartime inflation, the loss of Burmese rice and a cyclone left millions unable to buy food.
why: Sen's study of it showed that famine is often about the right to buy food, not the amount of food.

sources.cite: Sen, A. (1981). Poverty and Famines. Oxford University Press.

name: Great Chinese Famine
what: The Great Leap Forward pulled labour off farms while officials reported false harvests and grain was taken.
why: The deadliest famine in history.

sources.cite: Dikotter, F. (2010). Mao's Great Famine. Bloomsbury.
Yang, J. (2012). Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine, 1958-1962. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

name: Ethiopian famine of 1983-1985
what: Drought in the north, worsened by the Derg government's war against rebels and forced resettlement.
why: Television images of it led to Live Aid.

sources.cite: de Waal, A. (1991). Evil Days: Thirty Years of War and Famine in Ethiopia. Human Rights Watch.

name: Toba super-eruption
what: The largest known eruption of the last two million years, in Sumatra.
why: An old theory that it nearly wiped out humanity is now widely doubted; that dispute is itself a good lesson in evidence.

sources.cite: Williams, M. (2012). Did the 73 ka Toba super-eruption have an enduring effect? Quaternary International 269.

name: Thera (Minoan) eruption
what: A huge eruption that blew out the centre of Santorini and buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri.
why: Its date is fought over between radiocarbon and Egyptian chronology; its role in the Minoan decline is debated.

sources.cite: Friedrich, W. L. et al. (2006). Santorini eruption radiocarbon dated to 1627-1600 B.C. Science 312(5773).

name: Okmok eruption
what: An Alaskan eruption whose ash sits in Greenland ice from early 43 BCE.
why: McConnell et al. link the cold, wet years after it to famine and unrest in Rome and Egypt after Caesar's murder.

sources.cite: McConnell, J. R. et al. (2020). Extreme climate after massive eruption of Alaska's Okmok volcano in 43 BCE and effects on the late Roman Republic and Ptolemaic Kingdom. PNAS 117(27).

name: Eruption of Vesuvius
what: Vesuvius buried Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae.
why: Pliny the Younger's letters about it, and his uncle's death, are the first eyewitness account of an eruption.

sources.cite: Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16 and 6.20.

name: Volcanic winter of 536
what: Eruptions in 536 and 540 (probably one in Iceland, one in the tropics) dimmed the sun for over a year.
why: Byzantine writers saw the sun like the moon; the cold decade led straight into the Plague of Justinian.

sources.cite: Sigl, M. et al. (2015). Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years. Nature 523, 543-549.
Buntgen, U. et al. (2016). Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD. Nature Geoscience 9, 231-236.

name: Eldgja eruption
what: The largest lava flood in historical times, in southern Iceland.
why: Oppenheimer et al. suggest memories of it shaped the doomsday poem Voluspa and helped Iceland turn Christian.

sources.cite: Oppenheimer, C. et al. (2018). The Eldgja eruption: timing, long-range impacts and influence on the Christianisation of Iceland. Climatic Change 147.

name: Samalas eruption
what: One of the largest eruptions of the last few thousand years, on Lombok, found from ice cores before it was found on the ground.
why: It destroyed the Lombok capital Pamatan and is a candidate trigger for the Little Ice Age.

sources.cite: Lavigne, F. et al. (2013). Source of the great A.D. 1257 mystery eruption unveiled, Samalas volcano, Rinjani Volcanic Complex, Indonesia. PNAS 110(42).

name: Huaynaputina eruption
what: The largest eruption in South America in recorded history.
why: The cold summer of 1601 that followed across the northern hemisphere set off the Russian famine.

sources.cite: Verosub, K. L. and Lippman, J. (2008). Global impacts of the 1600 eruption of Peru's Huaynaputina volcano. Eos 89(15).

name: Tenmei eruption of Asama
what: A large eruption of Mount Asama in central Japan.
why: Its ash fell on farmland during an already failing run of harvests.

sources.cite: Kikuchi, I. (1997). Kinsei no kikin (Famines of early modern Japan); Jansen, M. (2000). The Making of Modern Japan. Harvard.

name: Laki eruption
what: An eight-month fissure eruption in Iceland that released a sulphur haze over Europe.
why: It killed about a fifth of Iceland and caused a toxic summer fog and a severe winter in Europe.

sources.cite: Thordarson, T. and Self, S. (2003). Atmospheric and environmental effects of the 1783-1784 Laki eruption. Journal of Geophysical Research 108(D1).
Wood, C. A. (1992). The climatic effects of the 1783 Laki eruption. In Harington (ed.), The Year Without a Summer?

name: Tambora eruption
what: The largest eruption in recorded history, on Sumbawa.
why: It caused the Year Without a Summer in 1816.

sources.cite: Oppenheimer, C. (2003). Climatic, environmental and human consequences of the largest known historic eruption: Tambora volcano (Indonesia) 1815. Progress in Physical Geography 27(2).

name: Krakatoa eruption
what: An eruption and tsunami in the Sunda Strait whose sound carried thousands of kilometres.
why: The first eruption followed worldwide by telegraph; its red sunsets were seen across the globe.

sources.cite: Simkin, T. and Fiske, R. S. (1983). Krakatau 1883: The Volcanic Eruption and Its Effects. Smithsonian.

name: Pinatubo eruption
what: An eruption in Luzon that put about 15 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere.
why: It cooled the planet by about half a degree for a year, the natural experiment that validated climate models.

sources.cite: Self, S. et al. (1996). The atmospheric impact of the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption. In Fire and Mud, USGS / PHIVOLCS.

name: End of the Green Sahara
what: The African Humid Period ended and a grassland of lakes and hippos dried into desert.
why: Herders moved to the Nile and the Sahel just as Egyptian civilisation took shape.

sources.cite: deMenocal, P. et al. (2000). Abrupt onset and termination of the African Humid Period. Quaternary Science Reviews 19.

name: 4.2-kiloyear drought
what: A centuries-long dry spell from the Mediterranean to the Indus.
why: Weiss linked it to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and the abandonment of northern Mesopotamian cities.

sources.cite: Weiss, H. et al. (1993). The genesis and collapse of third millennium North Mesopotamian civilization. Science 261(5124).

name: Late Bronze Age drought
what: A dry period in the eastern Mediterranean seen in pollen cores from Cyprus and Syria.
why: One of the stresses, with earthquakes, invasions and broken trade, behind the Late Bronze Age collapse.

sources.cite: Kaniewski, D. et al. (2013). Environmental roots of the Late Bronze Age crisis. PLoS ONE 8(8).
Cline, E. H. (2014). 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed. Princeton University Press.

name: Roman Climate Optimum
what: A warm, wet and stable period around the Mediterranean.
why: Harper argues it was a hidden partner in Rome's rise.

sources.cite: McCormick, M. et al. (2012). Climate change during and after the Roman Empire. Journal of Interdisciplinary History 43(2).
Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton University Press.

name: Late Antique Little Ice Age
what: A cold century after the eruptions of 536-547, seen in tree rings across Eurasia.
why: Buntgen et al. tie it to plague, migrations from the steppe and the upheavals of the seventh century.

sources.cite: Buntgen, U. et al. (2016). Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD. Nature Geoscience 9, 231-236.

name: Terminal Classic Maya droughts
what: A run of multi-year droughts in the Maya lowlands recorded in lake and cave sediments.
why: A leading explanation for the Classic Maya collapse, alongside endemic warfare.

sources.cite: Haug, G. H. et al. (2003). Climate and the collapse of Maya civilization. Science 299(5613).
Kennett, D. J. et al. (2012). Development and disintegration of Maya political systems in response to climate change. Science 338(6108).

name: Medieval Climate Anomaly
what: Warmer conditions around the North Atlantic, though not everywhere at once.
why: The Norse settled Greenland in it, and Europe's population grew fast.

sources.cite: Mann, M. E. et al. (2009). Global signatures and dynamical origins of the Little Ice Age and Medieval Climate Anomaly. Science 326(5957).

name: Angkor megadroughts
what: Decades of weak monsoons, broken by violent floods, recorded in Vietnamese cypress tree rings.
why: They may have wrecked the vast water system Angkor depended on.

sources.cite: Buckley, B. M. et al. (2010). Climate as a contributing factor in the demise of Angkor, Cambodia. PNAS 107(15).

name: Little Ice Age
what: A long cool period with especially cold phases in the 1600s, when the Thames froze and glaciers advanced.
why: Parker calls the 17th century a global crisis of war and revolt driven partly by this cold.

sources.cite: Mann, M. E. et al. (2009). Global signatures and dynamical origins of the Little Ice Age and Medieval Climate Anomaly. Science 326(5957).
Miller, G. H. et al. (2012). Abrupt onset of the Little Ice Age triggered by volcanism and sustained by sea-ice/ocean feedbacks. Geophysical Research Letters 39.
Parker, G. (2013). Global Crisis: War, Climate Change and Catastrophe in the Seventeenth Century. Yale University Press.

name: Late Ming drought
what: The worst drought in north China in five centuries, with locusts and epidemics.
why: It fed the rebellions that took Beijing in 1644.

sources.cite: Parker, G. (2013). Global Crisis: War, Climate Change and Catastrophe in the Seventeenth Century. Yale University Press.

name: El Nino of 1876-1878
what: One of the strongest El Nino events on record, failing monsoons across Asia, Africa and Brazil.
why: The common climate cause behind the famines of the late 1870s.

sources.cite: Davis, M. (2001). Late Victorian Holocausts: El Nino Famines and the Making of the Third World. Verso.

name: Dust Bowl
what: Drought and ploughed-up prairie turned the southern Plains into dust storms.
why: Two and a half million people left the Plains, the migration in The Grapes of Wrath.

sources.cite: Worster, D. (1979). Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s. Oxford University Press.

name: Sahel drought
what: Rains across the Sahel failed for nearly two decades.
why: Giannini et al. trace it to Atlantic and Indian Ocean temperatures rather than local overgrazing.

sources.cite: Giannini, A. et al. (2003). Oceanic forcing of Sahel rainfall on interannual to interdecadal time scales. Science 302(5647).

name: Industrial-era warming
what: Burning fossil fuels has warmed the planet by about 1.1 degrees since the late 19th century.
why: The fastest climate shift in this whole list, and the one Atlas will be asked about most.

sources.cite: IPCC (2021). Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers.

name: Late Bronze Age collapse
what: Palace states from Mycenae to Ugarit fell within a few decades.
why: Cline's case for a "perfect storm" of drought, quakes, raiders and broken trade is a model multi-lens story.

sources.cite: Cline, E. H. (2014). 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed. Princeton University Press.

name: Classic Maya collapse
what: The great southern lowland cities such as Tikal were abandoned.
why: Drought, war and overstretched kings all compete as explanations.

sources.cite: Kennett, D. J. et al. (2012). Development and disintegration of Maya political systems in response to climate change. Science 338(6108).

name: End of Norse Greenland
what: The last written record from Norse Greenland is a wedding in 1408; the settlements were empty soon after.
why: Cold, falling walrus-ivory prices and isolation all played a part.

sources.cite: Dugmore, A. J. et al. (2012). Cultural adaptation, compounding vulnerabilities and conjunctures in Norse Greenland. PNAS 109(10).

name: Pestis secunda
what: The first return of plague after the Black Death, remembered in England and France as the "children's plague".
why: It hit those born since 1348 hardest, so Europe's population could not bounce back; plague then returned every decade or so for 300 years.

sources.cite: Benedictow, O. J. (2004). The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History. Boydell Press.
Biraben, J.-N. (1975). Les hommes et la peste en France et dans les pays europeens et mediterraneens. Mouton.

name: Italian plague of 1629-1631
what: German and French armies fighting over Mantua brought plague into northern Italy, killing half of Milan and a third of Venice.
why: Alfani argues it explains why Italy fell behind northern Europe; Venice built Santa Maria della Salute to give thanks for its end.

sources.cite: Alfani, G. (2013). Plague in seventeenth-century Europe and the decline of Italy: an epidemiological hypothesis. European Review of Economic History 17(4).
Manzoni, A. (1827/1842). I promessi sposi (The Betrothed), chapters 31-35.

name: Naples plague of 1656
what: Plague killed around half of Naples, then one of Europe's largest cities, in a few months.
why: The single deadliest city outbreak of the 17th century.

sources.cite: Alfani, G. (2013). Plague in seventeenth-century Europe and the decline of Italy: an epidemiological hypothesis. European Review of Economic History 17(4).

name: Great Northern War plague
what: Plague moved with armies of the Great Northern War through Poland, Prussia, the Baltic, Stockholm and Copenhagen.
why: Copenhagen lost about a third of its people in 1711; it was the last great plague of northern Europe.

sources.cite: Frandsen, K.-E. (2010). The Last Plague in the Baltic Region 1709-1713. Museum Tusculanum Press.

name: Moscow plague of 1771
what: Plague came home with soldiers from the Russo-Turkish war and killed perhaps a fifth of Moscow.
why: When the archbishop removed a miracle-working icon to stop crowds gathering, a mob killed him in the Plague Riot.

sources.cite: Alexander, J. T. (1980). Bubonic Plague in Early Modern Russia: Public Health and Urban Disaster. Johns Hopkins University Press.

name: Typhus in the Grande Armee
what: Lice-borne typhus and dysentery destroyed much of Napoleon's army on the road to and from Moscow.
why: Mass graves in Vilnius dug up in 2001 showed typhus and trench fever in the soldiers' remains.

sources.cite: Talty, S. (2009). The Illustrious Dead: The Terrifying Story of How Typhus Killed Napoleon's Greatest Army. Crown; Raoult, D. et al. (2006) Journal of Infectious Diseases 193(1).
Zinsser, H. (1935). Rats, Lice and History. Little, Brown.

name: Second cholera pandemic
what: Cholera left Bengal again and for the first time reached Europe and North America.
why: Riots broke out from St Petersburg to Liverpool over rumours that doctors were killing the poor.

sources.cite: Pollitzer, R. (1959). Cholera. World Health Organization Monograph 43.
McGrew, R. E. (1965). Russia and the Cholera, 1823-1832. University of Wisconsin Press.
Rosenberg, C. E. (1962). The Cholera Years: The United States in 1832, 1849, and 1866. University of Chicago Press.

name: Broad Street cholera outbreak
what: An outbreak in Soho that John Snow traced to a single water pump on Broad Street.
why: His dot map is a founding moment of epidemiology and of data maps.

sources.cite: Snow, J. (1855). On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed. London.

name: African rinderpest panzootic
what: A cattle plague brought into the Horn of Africa killed most of the cattle from Ethiopia to South Africa.
why: Herding societies starved, and the famine and depopulation eased the European conquest of East and southern Africa.

sources.cite: Pankhurst, R. (1966). The Great Ethiopian Famine of 1888-1892. Journal of the History of Medicine 21(2); Spinage, C. A. (2003). Cattle Plague: A History. Springer.

name: Russian Civil War typhus
what: Typhus spread through armies, refugees and railways during the Russian Civil War.
why: Lenin said "either socialism defeats the louse, or the louse defeats socialism".

sources.cite: Patterson, K. D. (1993). Typhus and its control in Russia, 1870-1940. Medical History 37(4).

name: End of smallpox
what: The WHO campaign to eradicate smallpox, which had killed perhaps 300 million people in the 20th century alone.
why: The last natural case was Ali Maow Maalin in Merca, Somalia, in 1977; the only human disease ever eradicated.

sources.cite: Fenner, F. et al. (1988). Smallpox and Its Eradication. World Health Organization.

name: French famine of 1693-1694
what: A cold, wet 1692 and 1693 during the Maunder Minimum ruined French harvests.
why: About 1.3 million died, a larger share of France than died in the First World War.

sources.cite: Lachiver, M. (1991). Les annees de misere: la famine au temps du Grand Roi. Fayard.

name: Great Frost of 1709
what: The coldest European winter in 500 years froze the sea at Venice and killed winter wheat across France.
why: Some 600,000 died in France on top of the losses of the War of the Spanish Succession.

sources.cite: Lachiver, M. (1991). Les annees de misere: la famine au temps du Grand Roi. Fayard.

name: Kyoho famine
what: Locusts and cold destroyed rice crops in western Japan.
why: It led to the first great rice riot in Edo, against rice wholesalers, in 1733.

sources.cite: Kikuchi, I. (2000). Nihon no rekishi saigai: Edo kohen no jishi to kikin. And Jannetta, A. (1987). Epidemics and Mortality in Early Modern Japan. Princeton.

name: Tenpo famine
what: Cold summers wrecked harvests across Japan, worst in the northeast.
why: Oshio Heihachiro rose in revolt in Osaka in 1837; the shogunate's weak response is read as a step toward its fall.

sources.cite: Kikuchi, I. (2000). Nihon no rekishi saigai: Edo kohen no jishi to kikin. And Jannetta, A. (1987). Epidemics and Mortality in Early Modern Japan. Princeton.

name: Great Ethiopian famine
what: Rinderpest killed most of Ethiopia's cattle, then drought and locusts followed.
why: Pankhurst estimated a third of Ethiopia died; it is still called Kifu Qen, the evil days.

sources.cite: Pankhurst, R. (1966). The Great Ethiopian Famine of 1888-1892. Journal of the History of Medicine 21(2); Spinage, C. A. (2003). Cattle Plague: A History. Springer.

name: Persian famine of 1917-1919
what: Drought, wartime occupation and grain requisitioning by foreign armies left Persia starving.
why: Death estimates are among the most contested of any modern famine.

sources.cite: Majd, M. G. (2003). The Great Famine and Genocide in Persia, 1917-1919. University Press of America; Afary, J. (2004) review in Iranian Studies.

name: Russian famine of 1921-1922
what: Drought on the Volga after years of civil war and grain requisitions.
why: Herbert Hoover's American Relief Administration fed about ten million people a day at its peak.

sources.cite: Patenaude, B. M. (2002). The Big Show in Bololand: The American Relief Expedition to Soviet Russia in the Famine of 1921. Stanford University Press.

name: Siege of Leningrad famine
what: German and Finnish forces cut Leningrad off for 872 days.
why: Most of the dead starved, the largest loss of life in any modern city.

sources.cite: Reid, A. (2011). Leningrad: Tragedy of a City under Siege, 1941-44. Bloomsbury.

name: Dutch Hunger Winter
what: A German blockade of the western Netherlands in the winter of 1944-45.
why: Children conceived during it carried health effects for life, a founding case for epigenetics.

sources.cite: Lumey, L. H. et al. (2011). Prenatal famine and adult health. Annual Review of Public Health 32.

name: Biafran famine
what: Nigeria's blockade of secessionist Biafra during the civil war.
why: Images of it gave birth to modern humanitarian NGOs such as Medecins Sans Frontieres.

sources.cite: Heerten, L. (2017). The Biafran War and Postcolonial Humanitarianism. Cambridge University Press.

name: North Korean famine
what: The loss of Soviet aid and floods collapsed food distribution in North Korea.
why: Called the Arduous March at home; markets grew up in the gaps the state left.

sources.cite: Haggard, S. and Noland, M. (2007). Famine in North Korea: Markets, Aid, and Reform. Columbia University Press.

name: Somalia famine of 2011
what: Drought in the Horn of Africa in a war zone where al-Shabaab blocked aid.
why: Half of the dead were children under five.

sources.cite: Checchi, F. and Robinson, W. C. (2013). Mortality among populations of southern and central Somalia affected by severe food insecurity and famine during 2010-2012. FAO/FEWS NET.

name: Smallpox in the Inca Empire
what: A new disease, most likely smallpox, ran ahead of the Spanish down the Andes.
why: It killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir, starting the civil war that Pizarro walked into in 1532.

sources.cite: Cook, N. D. (1998). Born to Die: Disease and New World Conquest, 1492-1650. Cambridge University Press.
McNeill, W. H. (1976). Plagues and Peoples. Anchor.

name: Moscow Plague Riot
what: A crowd sacked the Chudov monastery and killed Archbishop Ambrosius during the plague.
why: Catherine II sent Grigory Orlov to restore order; plague riots recur wherever quarantine meets fear.

sources.cite: Alexander, J. T. (1980). Bubonic Plague in Early Modern Russia: Public Health and Urban Disaster. Johns Hopkins University Press.
Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 2.47-54.
Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome: Climate, Disease, and the End of an Empire. Princeton University Press.
McNeill, J. R. (2010). Mosquito Empires: Ecology and War in the Greater Caribbean, 1620-1914. Cambridge University Press.
Wood, C. A. (1992). The climatic effects of the 1783 Laki eruption. In Harington (ed.), The Year Without a Summer?
Dunning, C. S. L. (2001). Russia's First Civil War: The Time of Troubles and the Founding of the Romanov Dynasty. Penn State Press.
Talty, S. (2009). The Illustrious Dead: The Terrifying Story of How Typhus Killed Napoleon's Greatest Army. Crown; Raoult, D. et al. (2006) Journal of Infectious Diseases 193(1).
